Using the trap lines: each trap line in a brief names one wrong option, why it tempts, and the finding in the stem that rules it out.

edits.find: • A definition may be dated. Older sources, including this NBME explanation, set adolescent hypertension at the 95th percentile at every age. The current 2017 American Academy of Pediatrics guideline uses a fixed cutoff of 130/80 mm Hg from age 13. Confirming High Blood Pressure in an Adolescent
edits.with:
• A definition may be dated. Older sources, including this NBME explanation, set adolescent hypertension at the 95th percentile at every age. The current 2017 American Academy of Pediatrics guideline uses a fixed cutoff of 130/80 mm Hg from age 13. Confirming High Blood Pressure in an Adolescent
  • Every wrong option is the treatment of a look-alike. A slipped capital femoral epiphysis is keyed as internal fixation, beside abduction bracing and spica casting (hip dysplasia), traction (fracture) and physical therapy (strain). Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
  • The finding is described, never named. A boy with a red, tender sole 3 weeks after a nail went through his shoe has osteomyelitis, but the word never appears; the question asks only for the organism. Foot Puncture Wound Infection
  • Each negative in the stem closes one decoy. In a newborn with two flank masses, an uncomplicated pregnancy, good Apgar scores and a normal hematocrit close renal vein thrombosis, which leaves polycystic kidney disease. Abdominal Mass in a Young Child
  • One noun at different sites makes a location question. A virilized 10-year-old girl is offered adrenal, ovarian and pituitary adenoma. A high dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) with a normal testosterone and a normal pelvic ultrasound places the source in the adrenal. Precocious Puberty
  • A disease usually taught in its severe form appears mild. Posterior urethral valves appear in a well, feeding newborn with no Potter features, among four other causes of prenatal hydronephrosis. The thick bladder wall and a dribbling stream place the level. Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence
  • The key is an umbrella term. A soft newborn murmur spreading to the lung fields and axilla is peripheral pulmonary stenosis, keyed as pulmonary stenosis because the specific name is not offered. Innocent vs Pathologic Murmurs
  • The common answer is left off, and a planted sign fits a decoy. A 16-year-old smoker with past asthma admissions and severe hyperinflation is keyed as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency because asthma is not an option. Clubbing and yellow sputum pull toward Kartagener syndrome. Asthma vs. COPD
  • A prevention lead-in skips the diagnosis. A recent immigrant with a rash that starts on the face is asked which vaccine would have prevented it. Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine prevents both measles and rubella, so the two need not be separated. When the stem reads as rubella and the explanation teaches measles, the stem sets the facts. Exanthems in a Child
  • The options are an age ladder, and the date is a cue. A 4-month-old seen in October is offered rotavirus, influenza, MMR, chickenpox and shingles. October fits influenza, but only rotavirus among the options is due at 4 months. Chickenpox and shingles are one virus listed twice. Vaccines at the Infant Visits
  • The clue sits in a relative. A boy with recurrent abscesses, osteomyelitis and pneumonia has a maternal uncle who died of fungal pneumonia, which points to X-linked chronic granulomatous disease. The key is written as impaired microbicidal activity. Recurrent Abscesses and Granulomas
  • Nine options form a lab grid. An 18-month-old with poor growth, no vomiting or diarrhea, a normal blood pressure, low potassium, a normal-gap acidosis and an alkaline urine is offered nine causes of a potassium problem. Each option sits in one cell of potassium (high or low), acid-base (acidosis or alkalosis) and blood pressure (high or normal); only renal tubular acidosis fills the low-potassium, acidosis, normal-pressure cell. Bartter syndrome appears under its tissue name, juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia. Hypokalemia with Acidosis in a Child
